video_title: How to Spot the Next Big Trade Before Wall Street
gist: Guest Chris Camillo (social-arbitrage investor) explains his conversational-data and data-matrix method, says Google Trends has been corrupted by AI queries since summer 2025 (forcing a Lululemon exit), and dissects his ~$11M Amazon earnings options trade driven by a bet that Jassy would defuse capex fears as Microsoft had. He also advocates concentrated levered accounts for long horizons, calls humanoid robotics years away, and flags autonomous drone warfare as a key AI risk.

insights.claim: Chris Camillo argues conversational data (e.g., TikTok comments, developer forums) is the earliest detectable signal of behavior change because people talk about purchases before and during them, ahead of transactional data like credit-card swipes that most hedge funds rely on.
insights.speaker: Chris Camillo
insights.so_what: Source earliest-stage signals from free organic conversation rather than paid transaction panels that are already priced.
insights.quote: conversational data will always be the earliest data point an investor will ever have access to

insights.claim: Conversational data is highly interpretable and has no historical correlation to revenue, so Camillo treats it as one input and builds a matrix of ~15 other data points (search, web traffic, store-manager interviews, card data); the count of aligning data points sets trade conviction.
insights.speaker: Chris Camillo
insights.so_what: Size positions by the number of independent, aligned data sources, not by the strength of any one signal.
insights.quote: you want to generally see how many aligning data points exist, right? And and that defines the degree of conviction you have in a trade

insights.claim: Camillo says he invested in Amazon roughly 13 years ago on the AWS thesis after observing developers talking about moving to the cloud.
insights.speaker: Chris Camillo
insights.so_what: Practitioner chatter (developers, engineers) can front-run enterprise adoption trends, not just consumer ones.

insights.claim: Camillo suggests a current use of conversational data is tracking employees at incumbent companies talking about their AI usage to measure the real speed of AI adoption across the economy.
insights.speaker: Chris Camillo
insights.so_what: Employee-level chatter on AI use is a potential leading indicator of enterprise AI adoption and AI vendor revenue.

insights.claim: For deep dives Camillo buys Nielsen and hedge-fund data and reads years of niche forums of a company's customers (e.g., engineer Reddit threads, HVAC trade forums going back two years) before putting 10-20% of net worth into options.
insights.speaker: Chris Camillo
insights.so_what: Customer-forum diligence is an under-used edge for industrial/B2B names, not just consumer stocks.

themes.theme: Google Trends corrupted by AI queries

insights.claim: Camillo claims that in summer 2025 the entire Google Trends dataset was corrupted when AI (he believes ChatGPT) queries began being counted as Google searches, producing unprecedented midsummer spikes across many brands.
insights.speaker: Chris Camillo
insights.so_what: Any quant or alt-data model using Google Trends since mid-2025 may be contaminated; check for regime breaks.
insights.quote: the entire Google Trend data set had been corrupted by AI AI queries

insights.claim: Camillo says he has largely stopped using Google Trends since summer 2025 and that the contamination is still ongoing, though few believed his warnings.
insights.speaker: Chris Camillo
insights.so_what: A once-core alt-data source for retail and quant investors may be structurally degraded.
insights.quote: I essentially have more or less not used Google Trends since last summer because of this

insights.claim: Camillo took a heavy long on Lululemon based on record Google Trends spikes, then exited about 10 days later when no other data source corroborated it and unrelated queries spiked at the same time; Lululemon then got 'destroyed' on earnings that quarter.
insights.speaker: Chris Camillo
insights.so_what: Cross-validation against unrelated control queries is a practical test for data-feed corruption.

insights.claim: Camillo argues one of the hardest and most important investor skills is exiting a public, vocal thesis when new information invalidates it, even at a loss; he says most investors and especially content creators cannot do this.
insights.speaker: Chris Camillo
insights.so_what: Treat public commitment to a thesis as a bias risk; pre-define invalidation data.
insights.quote: Most people see you when you get in a trade. They rarely listen to you when you get out of a trade

themes.theme: Anatomy of the Amazon earnings options trade

insights.claim: Camillo says he made about $10-11 million in one day on levered Amazon options into earnings after being down about $8 million in prior weeks, including a seven-figure 100% loss on options that expired the week before after Microsoft earnings.
insights.speaker: Chris Camillo
insights.so_what: Illustrates path risk of expiration timing even with a correct thesis.
insights.quote: I think I was down 8 million and I made 11 million

insights.claim: Camillo's marginal driver was not an AWS revenue beat, which the Street expected, but his read that CEO Andy Jassy would address the capex worry head-on, as Microsoft had done and been rewarded for three days earlier.
insights.speaker: Chris Camillo
insights.so_what: Identify the narrative the stock is actually trading on (here capex fears) and use peer earnings calls to predict management messaging.
insights.quote: that was not the marginal driver of my conviction that day

insights.claim: According to Camillo, Amazon raised capex guidance from $200 billion to $220 billion while stating demand exists for every dollar and that most commitments are held flexibly until final equipment deliveries, hedging scenarios such as an AI lab like Anthropic or OpenAI failing.
insights.speaker: Chris Camillo
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler capex keeps rising, but management is signaling optionality to cancel late-stage deliveries; a counterparty-failure risk is now openly addressed.
insights.quote: we're going to increase capex again from 200 to 220 billion

insights.claim: Capex concern had been the number one issue that hit Amazon stock the prior quarter and for four months, making its resolution the key catalyst.
insights.speaker: Chris Camillo
insights.so_what: When one issue dominates investor pushback, management's handling of it outweighs headline beats.

insights.claim: Even at peak conviction Camillo still assigned roughly a 20% chance of failure, citing overnight macro risk such as what Trump might say about Iran.
insights.speaker: Chris Camillo
insights.so_what: Explicit probability framing keeps sizing honest even on best ideas.
insights.quote: there was still like an only an 80% shot of that trade working

insights.claim: Camillo says trades with this level of conviction come only one to five times a year (possibly zero), and requires around 100 hours of research before risking ~10% of liquid net worth on short-dated options.
insights.speaker: Chris Camillo
insights.so_what: Rare high-conviction setups justify concentrated sizing; scarcity is why he deems not taking them 'irresponsible'.

insights.claim: Camillo prefers the nuance and complexity of single stock earnings reactions over isolating a metric via prediction markets, because his edge lies in guessing the marginal driver of the day, though he likes prediction markets in principle.
insights.speaker: Chris Camillo
insights.so_what: Prediction markets may strip out the narrative complexity where discretionary edge exists.

insights.claim: Camillo says he has generated 50-80% annualized returns for 18 years in his primary account, which is typically 30-70% levered and at times 100% levered plus options.
insights.speaker: Chris Camillo
insights.so_what: His track record is a concentrated, levered, tech-correlated strategy, not a diversified one.

insights.claim: Camillo treats being only 30% levered with no options as the equivalent of holding cash, since spare margin lets him lever up repeatedly even after two or three wrong calls.
insights.speaker: Chris Camillo
insights.so_what: Dry powder can be unused borrowing capacity rather than literal cash.

insights.claim: Camillo argues retail investors underappreciate concentration and leverage and should keep a separate dedicated account where responsible leverage is used, accepting occasional 70% drawdowns (he took one this summer) for 2-3x market returns over decades.
insights.speaker: Chris Camillo
insights.so_what: Bucket accounts by objective; reject the Wall Street dogma of uncorrelated returns and drawdown avoidance for a long-horizon growth bucket.
insights.quote: There's nothing wrong with a 70% draw down if over time you're going to generate two to 3x market returns

insights.claim: Camillo cites backtests and white papers claiming a 3x leveraged S&P 500 or Nasdaq ETF returned about 1.8x the market over 80 years despite massive drawdowns, and estimates the wipeout risk at about 0.1-0.2%.
insights.speaker: Chris Camillo
insights.so_what: Pitch for broad-index leveraged ETFs as a long-horizon tool; the wipeout probability estimate is his own and unverified.
insights.quote: Basically, the returns are 1.8x the market

insights.claim: Camillo argues a long-horizon account should be deliberately correlated to technology and the 'industry of intelligence', which he believes will be all that matters in a few decades.
insights.speaker: Chris Camillo
insights.so_what: Implies sustained overweight in AI/tech buildout exposure.

insights.claim: Camillo, who says he is invested in about 180 early-stage companies, calls embodied AI and humanoid robotics the biggest thing humanity will see but says it is years away: deployment of generalized robots is exceptionally hard and will play out slowly over 5-10 years, like autonomous cars.
insights.speaker: Chris Camillo
insights.so_what: Fade near-term humanoid hype while positioning for a long-dated payoff.
insights.quote: Don't believe what all the hype tells you

insights.claim: Camillo says the AI wave since ChatGPT is the largest and fastest change he has seen, and the bigger and faster the change, the bigger the investment opportunity.
insights.speaker: Chris Camillo
insights.so_what: Rate of change, not only magnitude, defines opportunity size.

insights.claim: Camillo is less worried about AI turning against humans than about bad actors using democratized intelligence, especially autonomous drone fleets in the millions that could erode America's defense advantage; he says autonomous warfare is not even in the first inning.
insights.speaker: Chris Camillo
insights.so_what: Autonomous drones and counter-drone defense are a structural theme; US military edge may erode.
insights.quote: we're in like not even in the first inning of autonomous warfare

insights.claim: Pompliano relays an unverified report that Iran used Claude to upload war plans and that Anthropic turned the information over to the government.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: AI labs are becoming de facto intelligence/compliance actors; unconfirmed.

insights.claim: Camillo says over half of his biggest trades in the last eight or nine years were surfaced by a small network of obsessive retail investors, after which he runs his own process; he advises others to find such people on X and steal ideas rather than copy trade.
insights.speaker: Chris Camillo
insights.so_what: Curated networks of obsessive independent researchers are an underpriced idea source.
insights.quote: steal, don't copy trade me, but steal my ideas and then do your own research

insights.claim: Camillo tells hedge funds they underestimate a subset of retail investors in two ways: they are smarter and have more money than assumed.
insights.speaker: Chris Camillo
insights.so_what: Retail flow and research can drive price discovery in names institutions overlook.
insights.quote: They are smarter than you think and they got way more money than you think

insights.claim: Camillo cites Bloom Energy as a conviction trade held for two years against short sellers and skeptics, which went from about $30 to $300 in about 15 months.
insights.speaker: Chris Camillo
insights.so_what: Example of a heavily shorted, disbelieved AI-power name re-rating tenfold.
insights.quote: here is Bloom from 30 to 300 you know in what 15 months

insights.claim: Pompliano argues individual investors are advantaged by having no investment committees, LPs or position-size limits, and by investing their own money, which breeds 'only the paranoid survive' discipline.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Structural freedom from mandates lets individuals pursue concentrated, cross-asset opportunities institutions cannot.
